stem: Matching: Micromolecules vs Macromolecules. Classify each molecule.
answer:
The pairings:

MoleculeClass

NucleobasesMicromolecule
ProteinsMacromolecule
Nucleic acidMacromolecule
Fatty acidMicromolecule
MineralsMicromolecule
LipidsMacromolecule
VitaminsMicromolecule

From 01 - Biochemistry. Micromolecules are the small units combined to build macromolecules, plus the small “others” the cell needs.

  • Micromolecules: nucleobases (the lecture lists nucleotides as the essential unit), fatty acids, minerals and vitamins, the last two among the lecture's “others” with metabolites, cofactors, metals and water.
  • Macromolecules: the four the lecture opens with - carbohydrates (polysaccharides of hundreds of sugars), proteins (chains of amino acids), nucleic acids and lipids.

The trap is fatty acid vs lipid: the fatty acid is the simplest building block, and the lipid is the class it builds.
note: Answer key: Micro B, E, F, H; Macro A, C, D, G.

stem: Matching: DNA vs. RNA. Match each feature with DNA or RNA.
answer:
The pairings:

FeatureNucleic acid
Relatively StableDNA
UracilRNA
Double StrandedDNA
ThymineDNA
Degraded quicklyRNA

Translated into proteinRNA

From 01 - Biochemistry. The lecture contrasts the two nucleic acids on strandedness, stability and bases.

  • DNA: double stranded, sturdy and relatively stable, and uses thymine.
  • RNA: single stranded, degraded quickly, and uses uracil in place of thymine. It is RNA that is translated into protein, read in three-letter codons.

The lecture puts that stability gap to work in sample prep: an enzyme that quickly breaks down the weaker RNA leaves the more stable DNA behind.

stem: Matching: Hematoxylin vs. Eosin. Match each property with its stain.
answer:
The pairings:

PropertyStain
BasicHematoxylin
AcidicEosin
Stains acids blueHematoxylin
Stains bases pinkEosin

From 03 - Histology and Tissue Types. Each dye has the opposite charge of what it stains.

  • Hematoxylin is the basic stain, and it stains acids blue: DNA, so nuclei come out blue.
  • Eosin is the acidic stain, and it stains bases pink: cytoplasmic proteins.

The trap is putting “acidic” and “stains acids” together. H&E is the principal stain in histology because it is quick and cheap and still shows a great deal of microscopic anatomy.

stem: Matching: Yes vs. No. For each change, choose Yes or No.

items.left: Increase the amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum
Drastically change cell shape to accommodate a functional need
Establish open pores on the cell surface to allow free passage of small and large molecules

answer:
The pairings:

ChangeYes or No
Increase the amount of rough endoplasmic reticulumYes
Drastically change cell shape to accommodate a functional needYes
Increase cell sizeYes
Eliminate the cell nucleusYes
Increase cell surface areaYes
Establish open pores on the cell surface to allow free passage of small and large moleculesNo
  • Increase the amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum - Yes, B‐cells and others have extensive endoplasmic reticulum networks for protein production.
  • Drastically change cell shape to accommodate a functional need - Yes, some cells like motor neurons can be up to 1 meter in length for electrical stimulation of a muscle fiber.
  • Increase cell size - Yes, skeletal muscle cells fuse to become multinucleated single large cells that are up to 30 cm in length.
  • Eliminate the cell nucleus - Yes, eye lens fiber cells become enucleated to allow undisrupted light to reach the retina.
  • Increase cell surface area - Yes, many epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal track have microvilli to increase surface area for absorption.
  • Establish open pores on the cell surface to allow free passage of small and large molecules - No, cells that have open pores will lose intracellular integrity and die, but cells due have channels that selectively regulate the passage of small molecules.
note: Answer gives Yes/No per item A-F (five Yes, F No).

Rich in undifferentiated mesenchymal cellsEmbryonic CT
Encapsulates many organsDense Irregular CT
Energy storage for newbornsBrown Fat

From 06 - Connective Tissue.

  • Low in cellular components - dense regular CT: packed with type I collagen, only fibroblasts in rows, little room for anything else.
  • Rich in undifferentiated mesenchymal cells - embryonic CT: embryonic CT is mesenchyme - pluripotent cells that give rise to fibroblasts, adipocytes, osteoblasts and more.
  • Encapsulates many organs - dense irregular CT: forms most organ capsules and the reticular dermis.
  • Energy storage for newborns - brown fat (multilocular, mitochondria-rich) is abundant in newborns for energy and thermoregulation.
  • Highly cellular tissue - white fat: white adipose tissue is described in the overview as highly cellular (unilocular adipocytes).
  • Typically found under the epithelium - loose CT: lies under epithelia and carries vessels and nerves.

From 06 - Connective Tissue. Each description names one bone structure from the lecture.

  • Secretes osteoid = osteoblasts (secrete bone matrix on demand, start mineralization with alkaline phosphatase).
  • Processes from osteocytes = canaliculi, where gap junctions pass nutrients.
  • Multinucleated, digests mineralized bone = osteoclasts (fused monocytes/macrophages, up to 30 nuclei, in Howship's lacunae).

  • Fully differentiated, embedded in bone = osteocytes, derived from osteoblasts.
  • Collagen from the periosteum = Sharpey's fibres, projecting into the outer lamellae.

stem: Match each statement with the body fluid compartment it describes.

items.left: It is considered the internal environment

answer:
The pairings:

StatementCompartment
Corresponds to 3/4th of the ECFInterstitial fluid
Corresponds to 1/3rd of the TBWExtracellular fluid
Corresponds to 1/4th of the ECFPlasma
Corresponds to 2/3rd of the TBWIntracellular fluid
It is rich in PotassiumIntracellular fluid
It is considered the internal environmentExtracellular fluid

From 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis). Total body water splits 2/3 intracellular, 1/3 extracellular, and the ECF splits again 3/4 interstitial, 1/4 plasma.

  • 3/4 of ECF = interstitial fluid; 1/4 of ECF = plasma.
  • 1/3 of TBW = ECF; 2/3 of TBW = ICF.
  • Rich in potassium = ICF: K+ is the main intracellular ion (about 150 vs 5 mmol/L outside), while Na+, Cl- and Ca2+ dominate outside.
  • The internal environment = ECF, the fluid bathing the cells that homeostasis holds constant.

The fractions nest: a fraction of the ECF is never a fraction of total body water.

stem: Match the following statements with the correct terms.

items.left: The signal is aimed to a local (nearby) target
The signal targets its own cell

The signal is transmitted via direct contact with the target

answer:
The pairings:

StatementType of signalling
The signal is aimed to a local (nearby) targetParacrine signaling
The signal targets its own cellAutocrine signaling
The signal is aimed to a long-distance targetLong distance signaling
The signal is transmitted via direct contact with the targetCell-cell contact signaling

From 08 - Cellular Communication. The four modes are named for the distance the signal travels and the route it takes.

  • Nearby target = paracrine: messengers act over short distances so neighbours coordinate locally.
  • Own cell = autocrine: the ligand binds receptors on the cell that released it, which the lecture links to cancer and metastasis.
  • Long-distance target = long-distance signalling, i.e. endocrine: hormones carried to target cells in the bloodstream.
  • Direct contact = cell-cell contact signalling: gap junctions, or surface proteins binding and changing conformation.

answer:
The pairings:

DescriptionTerm
Phagocytic cells that become activated in the CNS traumaMicroglial cells
Bridging cells between axons and blood vessels in the CNSAstrocytes
Disease caused by the loss of myelination in the CNSMultiple Sclerosis
Myelinating cells found in the PNSSchwann Cells
Neuronal outgrowths that occur when an axon is severedAxonal sprouts

From 07 - Nerves. Each description names one cell or event from the lecture's glial-cell and nerve-regeneration notes.

  • Phagocytes activated by CNS injury = microglia: migratory, and they turn phagocytic when the CNS is damaged.
  • Bridging axons and blood vessels = astrocytes: a scaffold between capillaries, fibres and neurons that maintains the blood-brain barrier.
  • Loss of CNS myelin = multiple sclerosis, demyelination of oligodendrocyte myelin.

stem: Match the movement of each ion with the type of change that it promotes in the membrane potential.
answer:
The pairings:

Ion movementChange in membrane potential
Ca+2 entryDepolarization
Cl- entryHyperpolarization
K+ exitHyperpolarization
Na+ entryDepolarization

From 08 - Cellular Communication. Depolarization moves the membrane potential toward zero or positive and hyperpolarization moves it more negative, so what matters is whether the charge crossing is net positive in or positive out.

  • Depolarization: Ca2+ entry and Na+ entry both bring positive charge in. Their equilibrium potentials (about +135 and +60 mV) sit far above -70 mV.
  • Hyperpolarization: Cl- entry brings negative charge in, and K+ exit takes positive charge out. This is the K+ efflux behind repolarization and the undershoot after an action potential.

A common slip: an ion leaving has the opposite effect of the same ion entering.
note: Key A (depolarization) - I, IV; B (hyperpolarization) - II, III.

stem: Match the change in the ion channel configuration with the corresponding phase of an action potential.

items.left: Closing of the inactivation gate of the sodium channels
Opening of the activation gate of the sodium channels

answer:
The pairings:

Ion channel changePhase of the action potential
Closing of the potassium channelsHyperpolarization phase
Closing of the inactivation gate of the sodium channelsPeak of an action potential
Opening of the activation gate of the sodium channelsDepolarization or rising phase
Opening of potassium channels (fully opened)Repolarization or falling phase

Please note that there is an overlap between the change in configuration of the ion channels and the phase of an action potential. For example, at the peak of an action potential, the inactivation gate of the sodium channels is closing at the same time that the potassium channels are becoming fully opened. Also, the closing of the potassium channels happens during the hyperpolarization phase but this is not what led to this phase.

The pelvis is _________ to the skull.
The muscles are __________ to the skin.

answer:
The pairings:

StatementTerm of reference
The heart is located ________ to the diaphragm.Superior
The ankle is located ________ to the knee.Distal
The thumb is located ________ to the index finger.Lateral
The spinal cord is _________ to the belly button.Posterior
The heart is ________ to the lung.Medial
The shoulder is _________ to the elbow.Proximal
The pelvis is _________ to the skull.Inferior
The muscles are __________ to the skin.Deep

From 09 - Anatomy. Every pair is read in the anatomical position.

  • Heart / diaphragm: superior, toward the head. Pelvis / skull: inferior.
  • Ankle / knee: distal, further from the trunk. Shoulder / elbow: proximal, toward the trunk.
  • Thumb / index finger: lateral. With the palms forward, the thumb is furthest from the midline.
  • Spinal cord / umbilicus: posterior, dorsal.
  • Heart / lung: medial, nearer the midline.
  • Muscles / skin: deep, further in from the surface.

Proximal/distal apply to the limbs; superior/inferior to the axial body.

From 09 - Anatomy. The lecture's four laterality terms:

From 10 - Body System Organization. The musculoskeletal system supports the body, allows motion and protects the vital organs. Its table divides the jobs among the parts.

  • Cartilage = smooth articulating surfaces: articular hyaline cartilage gives a smooth surface for joint movement.
  • Bones = structure and protection.
  • Ligaments = bone to bone.
  • Joints = enable movement between bones.
  • Tendons = muscle to bone. Tendons and ligaments are both dense regular connective tissue, type I collagen in rows (06 - Connective Tissue).
  • Muscles = produce movement at joints.

Tendon vs ligament is the classic trap: tendon joins muscle to bone, ligament joins bone to bone.

stem: Classify the following inputs and outputs as either somatosensory (SS), visceral sensory (VS), somatic motor (SM), or automatic motor (ANS).
answer:
The pairings:

Input or outputClassification
Stomach acheVisceral sensory (VS)
Pain from skinSomatosensory (SS)
Efferent innervation of glandAutonomic motor (ANS)
Efferent innervation of gluteus maximusSomatic motor (SM)

From 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System. Sort each item on two axes: sensory (afferent) or motor (efferent), then body wall (somatic) or viscera (visceral/autonomic).

  • Stomach ache = visceral sensory: pain from a viscus, carried by visceral afferents, which is why it feels diffuse and achy and is often referred.
  • Pain from skin = somatosensory: somatic afferents bring sensation from the body wall (skin, skeletal muscle, joints) in through the dorsal root.
  • Efferent to a gland = autonomic motor: the ANS acts on viscera, glands, smooth and cardiac muscle.
  • Efferent to gluteus maximus = somatic motor: impulses to skeletal muscle leave through the ventral root.
note: Key A-VS, B-SS, C-ANS, D-SM.

stem: Match the following principles with their definitions.

items.left: A mutant protein is produced and adversely affects the function of the normal protein
A single functioning allele of a gene is not sufficient to produce a normal phenotype
Proportion of individuals with a mutation who show clinical signs of the disorder
A pathogenic variant in one gene can cause multiple effects in different organs

answer:
The pairings:

DefinitionPrinciple
A mutant protein is produced and adversely affects the function of the normal proteinDominant negative
A single functioning allele of a gene is not sufficient to produce a normal phenotypeHaploinsufficiency
Proportion of individuals with a mutation who show clinical signs of the disorderPenetrance
A pathogenic variant in one gene can cause multiple effects in different organsPleiotropy
The mutation results in increased activity of the normal gene productGain of function

From 02 - Genetics. The key matches the note's dominant-inheritance terms:

  • Dominant negative: the mutant protein interferes with the normal one from the other allele, as the mutant alpha chain does in severe osteogenesis imperfecta.
  • Haploinsufficiency: one working allele is not enough, as with ELN in Williams syndrome.
  • Gain of function: increased activity of the normal product, as in achondroplasia.
  • Pleiotropy: one gene, many organs, as with collagen in OI affecting bone, eyes, ears and joints.
  • Penetrance: the proportion of carriers who show clinical signs.

answer:

DescriptionTerm
Two different mutations on different alleles on same geneCompound heterozygotes
All of the offspring of an individual with an autosomal recessive disorderObligate heterozygotes
Two alleles of the same gene with the same variantHomozygote

From 02 - Genetics.

  • Compound heterozygote: two different variants on the two alleles of the same gene, the note's “trans” arrangement, which leaves no good copy and so causes recessive disease.
  • Homozygote: two alleles of the same gene carrying the same variant; affected.
  • Obligate heterozygotes: an affected person with an autosomal recessive disorder can only pass on a variant allele, so every child must be at least a carrier, whether or not they are tested.

From 06 - Connective Tissue. The keyed mapping matches the note's table exactly.

  • Dense irregular CT is found in most organ capsules and the reticular layer of the dermis; its type I and III collagen is woven into a mat, making it resilient and protective.

  • Loose CT sits under epithelia, carries vessels and nerves, and has poorly organized fibres.

From 06 - Connective Tissue.

  • White: the adult energy store and insulator; unilocular (one lipid vacuole per cell), which pushes the nucleus to the periphery; the cells can grow about 4× before dividing, and once divided are hard to clear.
  • Brown: abundant in newborns (2-5% of body weight) for thermoregulation; multilocular (many small droplets), so the nucleus stays central; packed with mitochondria, which is what makes it a heat generator.

The discriminator is locularity: one droplet displaces the nucleus, many droplets leave it central.

From 06 - Connective Tissue. The key matches the note's cartilage table.

  • Elastic cartilage (type II collagen plus elastin) is where shape must spring back: epiglottis, larynx, pinna and auditory canal.
  • Fibrocartilage (types I and II collagen, chondrocytes in parallel rows) resists compression: intervertebral discs, menisci, the jaw, tendon insertions.
  • Hyaline, the most common type (type II collagen, isogenous groups), forms the growth plates, ventral rib ends and the walls of the respiratory tree.

answer:
The pairings:

DescriptionBone cell type
Bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cellsOsteoprogenitor cells
Actively secrete bone matrixOsteoblast
Interconnected cellular network within the bone matrix and maintain its calcificationOsteocyte
Multinucleated cells which resorb bone and cartilage matrixOsteoclasts

From 06 - Connective Tissue. The four bone cells form a lineage plus one outsider.

  • Marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells = osteoprogenitor cells, in the periosteum and endosteum, which differentiate into osteoblasts during repair.
  • Actively secrete matrix = osteoblasts, which also start mineralization with alkaline phosphatase.
  • Interconnected network that maintains calcification = osteocytes: osteoblasts walled into matrix, linked by canaliculi, and mechanosensory.
  • Multinucleated cells that resorb matrix = osteoclasts, the outsider, fused from blood monocytes/macrophages rather than the mesenchymal line.
note: Key A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.
